gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: The SUVAT equation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives it to you. From rest, u = 0.

steps.done: 30 m/s. Remember to square root at the end.

gold.display: A motorbike accelerates from rest at 5 m/s² over 90 m. Calculate its final velocity. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\).

bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time: \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). Metres and seconds already, so no conversion.

bronze.display: A skateboarder travels 90 m in 15 seconds. Calculate the speed.

silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time, but the units are km and minutes. Convert to metres and seconds first.

steps.hint: Speed × time returns the distance in metres.

silver.display: A train travels 72 km in 20 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.

opener.label: Before any equations

steps.say: No equations yet, just common sense. You walk a 60 m corridor, end to end, and it takes 30 seconds. Spread the 60 m evenly across the 30 seconds.
That number, metres per second, is speed. You just did speed = distance ÷ time without being told. Now you speed up: over 4 seconds your speed climbs steadily from 2 m/s to 6 m/s.
steps.hint: Speed rose by 6 − 2 = 4 m/s, spread over 4 seconds.

steps.say: That steady gain, 1 metre per second every second, is acceleration. Two ideas, both just sharing a change over time: speed shares distance over time (\(v = \frac{s}{t}\)), acceleration shares change in speed over time (\(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\)). The rest of this lesson is those two, plus reading them off graphs.

opener.display:
A 60 m corridor.
You walk it, end to end, in 30 seconds.

steps: Choose the equation: speed \(v = s/t\), acceleration \(a = \Delta v/\Delta t\), or distance \(s = vt\).
Convert to base units first: metres, seconds and m/s (km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s).
For graphs: gradient of a distance-time graph = speed; area under a velocity-time graph = distance.
Substitute, calculate, and state the answer with its unit.
method_card.title: Speed, Acceleration and Graphs
method_card.content:
Speed is distance ÷ time (\(v = s/t\)); acceleration is change in speed ÷ time (\(a = \Delta v/\Delta t\)). Both need base units: metres and seconds.

On a distance-time graph the gradient gives the speed. On a velocity-time graph the gradient gives the acceleration and the area underneath gives the distance, found by splitting into triangles and rectangles.

The higher-tier equation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) links speed, acceleration and distance; it gives \(v^2\), so square root at the end. Slowing down counts as negative acceleration.

steps: Two equations may chain: find acceleration from \(F = ma\), then a speed from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives you the SUVAT equation.
That equation gives \(v^2\), so square root at the end. Slowing down means a is negative.
For a velocity-time graph, distance = area under the line: split into triangles and rectangles and add them.
gold.title: Gold: multi-step and graphs

example.question: A car accelerates from rest at 2 m/s² over 100 m. Find its final speed.

steps: Pick the right equation: speed \(v = \frac{s}{t}\), acceleration \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\), or distance \(s = vt\).
The values are already in metres, seconds and m/s, so substitute straight in and calculate.
Acceleration uses the change in speed (final minus start), not just the final speed. Slowing down is negative.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, values ready to use

example.question: A cyclist travels 100 m in 25 s. Calculate the speed.

steps: The values arrive in the wrong units: km, minutes, or km/h. Convert to metres and seconds before substituting.
Handy conversions: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 minute = 60 s, and km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s.
For uniform acceleration, distance = average speed × time, where average speed = (start + end) ÷ 2.
silver.title: Silver: convert the units first

example.question: A car travels 36 km in 20 minutes. Calculate the average speed in m/s.

exam_context.frequency: Very high: motion graphs and calculations appear on almost every Paper 1

gold.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as with u = 0, then square root.
gold.display: A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s². Calculate its velocity after travelling 150 m.

guided_steps.say: This uses the SUVAT equation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives you this equation or expects you to recall it. From rest, u = 0.

guided_steps.done: 30 m/s. The equation gives v², so square root at the end.

misconceptions.message: The equation gives v² = 0 + 2 × 3 × 150 = 900, so you must square root: v = √900 = 30 m/s, not 900 m/s.

gold.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as with final speed 0 and a negative acceleration.
gold.display: A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 4 m/s². Calculate the braking distance.

guided_steps.say: Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with u = 20 m/s, final v = 0 (it stops), and a = −4 m/s² (slowing). Check whether your board gives you this equation.

guided_steps.done: Braking distance = 50 m.

misconceptions.message: Deceleration means a = −4 m/s². With v = 0: 0 = 20² + 2 × (−4) × s = 400 − 8s, so s = 50 m. Using a = +4 gives −50 m, which is impossible for a distance.
v² = u² + 2as with v = 0: 0 = 400 − 8s, so 8s = 400 and s = 50 m.

gold.hint: Distance is the area under the graph: two triangles and a rectangle.
gold.display: The velocity-time graph shows a complete journey. Calculate the total distance travelled.

guided_steps.say: Distance = area under the velocity-time graph. Split into three parts: a triangle (0 to 6 s), a rectangle (6 to 8 s), and a triangle (8 to 14 s).

misconceptions.message: Three sections: triangle (0 to 6 s) = ½ × 6 × 15 = 45 m, rectangle (6 to 8 s) = 2 × 15 = 30 m, triangle (8 to 14 s) = ½ × 6 × 15 = 45 m; total 120 m. Forgetting the middle rectangle gives only 90 m.
Find the area under the graph, not the gradient. Split into triangles and rectangles.

gold.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as with u = 0 and a = 9.8, then rearrange for s.
gold.display: A stone is dropped from rest and hits the ground at 24.5 m/s. Calculate the height it fell from. Use \(g = 9.8\) m/s².

guided_steps.say: Falling from rest, so u = 0, and v = 24.5 m/s at the ground. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with a = g = 9.8 m/s². Check whether your board gives you this equation.

guided_steps.done: Matches 24.5². Height ≈ 30.6 m.

gold.hint: Find acceleration from F = ma, then use v² = u² + 2as.
gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 15 m/s. It accelerates over 100 m to reach a new speed. The resultant force on the car is 3600 N. Calculate the final speed of the car. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

guided_steps.say: Two equations. First get acceleration from \(F = ma\), then the final speed from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives you the second equation.

guided_steps.pre: Square root and round to 1 d.p.: v = √825 =
guided_steps.done: √825 = 28.72, which rounds to 28.7 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Work out √825, then give 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: First a = F ÷ m = 3600 ÷ 1200 = 3 m/s², then v² = u² + 2as = 225 + 600 = 825, so v = √825 = 28.7 m/s. Forgetting to add u² gives √600 = 24.5 m/s.
Two equations here: F = ma gives a = 3 m/s², then v² = u² + 2as gives the final speed.

gold.hint: Split into two phases; use the average speed for the accelerating part.
gold.display: A cyclist accelerates from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 seconds, then travels at a constant 10 m/s for another 7 seconds. Calculate the total distance covered in 10 seconds.

guided_steps.say: Split the journey into two phases. Phase 1: accelerating from 4 to 10 m/s over 3 s, use the average speed. Phase 2: constant 10 m/s for 7 s.

guided_steps.hint: Add the two speeds, then halve.

guided_steps.done: Distance = 91 m.

misconceptions.message: Two phases. Accelerating (0 to 3 s): average speed = (4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7 m/s, distance = 21 m. Constant (3 to 10 s): 10 × 7 = 70 m. Total = 91 m. Counting only the constant phase gives 70 m.
During the acceleration use the average speed (7 m/s), not 10 m/s. Using 10 m/s for the whole 10 s gives 100 m instead of 91 m.

bronze.hint: Speed is distance divided by time.
bronze.display: A cyclist travels 600 m in 40 seconds. Calculate their speed.

guided_steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time: \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). The values are already in metres and seconds, so no conversion is needed.

guided_steps.done: 600 m, matching the distance. Speed = 15 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance.

misconceptions.message: Speed = distance ÷ time = 600 ÷ 40 = 15 m/s. Dividing time by distance (40 ÷ 600) is upside down.

bronze.hint: Acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time.
bronze.display: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 10 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). Change in speed means final minus starting.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the change in speed by the time.

guided_steps.done: 20 m/s gained, matching 25 − 5. Acceleration = 2 m/s².
guided_steps.hint: Acceleration × time should return the change in speed.

misconceptions.message: Use the change in speed, not the final speed: Δv = 25 − 5 = 20 m/s, so a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s². Using 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5 forgets to subtract the starting speed.

bronze.hint: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
bronze.display: A runner moves at a constant speed of 4 m/s for 30 seconds. Calculate the distance covered.

guided_steps.say: Distance = speed × time: rearranged from \(v = \frac{s}{t}\) to \(s = vt\). Units are already m/s and s.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4 m/s, the given speed. Distance = 120 m.
guided_steps.hint: Distance ÷ time should return the speed.

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 4 × 30 = 120 m. Do not divide.

bronze.hint: Find the change in speed, then divide by the time; the deceleration is its size.
bronze.display: A train decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the deceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). Slowing down gives a negative value, and the deceleration is its size.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the change by the time; keep the minus.

guided_steps.done: The minus sign just means slowing down. Deceleration = 5 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Δv = 10 − 30 = −20 m/s, so a = −20 ÷ 4 = −5 m/s². The minus just means slowing down; the deceleration is its size, 5 m/s².

bronze.hint: On a distance-time graph, speed is the gradient: rise over run.
bronze.display: The distance-time graph shows a journey. Calculate the speed during the first 15 seconds.

guided_steps.say: On a distance-time graph, speed = gradient = rise ÷ run. Read the rise and run over the first 15 seconds.

guided_steps.hint: Read the graph at t = 15 s.

guided_steps.done: 60 m in 15 s, matching the graph. Speed = 4 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance.

bronze.equation_hint: Gradient of a distance-time graph = speed

misconceptions.message: Speed = gradient = rise ÷ run = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 m/s. Doing run ÷ rise (15 ÷ 60 = 0.25) inverts the gradient.

bronze.hint: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
bronze.display: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s. How far does it travel in 0.5 seconds?

guided_steps.say: Distance = speed × time: \(s = vt\). Units are m/s and s already.

guided_steps.done: Back to 340 m/s. Distance = 170 m.

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 340 × 0.5 = 170 m. Dividing (340 ÷ 0.5 = 680) uses the wrong operation.

bronze.hint: From rest the starting speed is 0; acceleration is the change in speed over time.
bronze.display: A bus accelerates from rest to 18 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). From rest means the starting speed is 0.

guided_steps.hint: Final minus starting; from rest the start is 0.
Divide the change by the time.

guided_steps.done: 18 m/s gained, matching from rest to 18. Acceleration = 3 m/s².
guided_steps.hint: Acceleration × time returns the change in speed.

misconceptions.message: From rest means u = 0, so Δv = 18 − 0 = 18 m/s and a = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s².

bronze.hint: Rearrange distance = speed × time to time = distance ÷ speed.
bronze.display: How long does it take a car travelling at 20 m/s to cover 500 m?

guided_steps.say: Start from \(s = vt\) and rearrange for time: \(t = \frac{s}{v}\). Units are m and m/s already.

guided_steps.done: 500 m covered, matching. Time = 25 s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange s = vt to t = s ÷ v = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 s.

silver.hint: Convert km to metres and minutes to seconds before dividing.
silver.display: A car travels 54 km in 30 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.

guided_steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time, but first convert to base units: metres and seconds.

guided_steps.done: 54,000 m = 54 km. Speed = 30 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance in metres.

misconceptions.message: Convert first: 54 km = 54,000 m and 30 min = 1800 s, so v = 54,000 ÷ 1800 = 30 m/s. Leaving time in minutes (54,000 ÷ 30 = 1800) is a unit slip.

silver.hint: Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6, then find the change in speed over time.
silver.display: A car travelling at 108 km/h brakes and stops in 5 seconds. Calculate the deceleration in m/s².

guided_steps.say: First convert 108 km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. The car stops, so the final speed is 0.

guided_steps.hint: Stops, so the final speed is 0: 0 − 30.
Divide the change by the time; keep the minus.

guided_steps.done: The minus means slowing. Deceleration = 6 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Convert first: 108 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s. Δv = 0 − 30 = −30 m/s, so a = −30 ÷ 5 = −6 m/s²; deceleration = 6 m/s². Using 108 ÷ 5 = 21.6 skips the conversion.
To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6: 108 ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s.

silver.hint: Distance is the area under the graph: split into a triangle and a rectangle.
silver.display: The velocity-time graph shows a car's journey. Calculate the total distance travelled in 20 seconds.

guided_steps.say: On a velocity-time graph, distance = area under the line. Split it into a triangle (0 to 10 s) and a rectangle (10 to 20 s).

guided_steps.pre: Cross-check with average speed: mean speed = 15 m/s over 20 s gives 15 × 20 =
guided_steps.done: Both routes give 300 m. Distance = 300 m.
guided_steps.hint: The mean of a 0 to 20 climb then a hold at 20 is 15 m/s.

silver.equation_hint: Area under a velocity-time graph = distance

misconceptions.message: Split the area: triangle (0 to 10 s) = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m, rectangle (10 to 20 s) = 10 × 20 = 200 m, total 300 m. Treating the whole graph as one triangle (½ × 20 × 20 = 200) misses the flat top.
Distance is the area under a velocity-time graph, not the gradient. Split it into a triangle and a rectangle.

silver.hint: Distance = average speed × time; average speed = (start + end) ÷ 2.
silver.display: A car accelerates uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels. (Hint: average speed × time)

guided_steps.say: For uniform acceleration, distance = average speed × time. Average speed = (start + end) ÷ 2.

guided_steps.hint: Add the two speeds, then halve.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 14 m/s average. Distance = 56 m.
guided_steps.hint: Distance ÷ time returns the average speed.

misconceptions.message: For uniform acceleration use the average speed: (8 + 20) ÷ 2 = 14 m/s, so distance = 14 × 4 = 56 m. Using the final speed (20 × 4 = 80) overcounts.

silver.hint: Find the final speed first, then use the average speed to get the distance.
silver.display: A sprinter accelerates at 4 m/s² from rest. Calculate their speed after 3 seconds, and the distance covered.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. First find the final speed with \(v = u + at\), then use the average speed to get distance. Starting from rest, u = 0.

guided_steps.hint: Add start and end speeds, then halve.

guided_steps.pre: The question asks for distance, not speed. Distance (m) =
guided_steps.done: 18 m. Do not stop at the 12 m/s speed.

silver.equation_hint: \(v = u + at\) and average speed \(= \frac{u + v}{2}\)

misconceptions.message: v = u + at = 0 + 4 × 3 = 12 m/s is the speed, but the question asks for the distance: average speed = (0 + 12) ÷ 2 = 6 m/s, distance = 6 × 3 = 18 m.

silver.hint: To turn km/h into m/s, divide by 3.6.
silver.display: A car travels at 90 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.

guided_steps.say: Convert km/h to m/s. One route: turn km into metres and hours into seconds. 90 km/h means 90 km every hour.

guided_steps.done: Same answer. The ÷3.6 shortcut is just ×1000 then ÷3600. Speed = 25 m/s.

silver.equation_hint: Divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s

misconceptions.message: To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6: 90 ÷ 3.6 = 25 m/s. Multiplying by 3.6 (giving 324) goes the wrong way.

problem_bank.gold_description: Multi-step problems: chain two equations, use the SUVAT equation, or read a motion graph.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, all values already in metres, seconds and m/s. Substitute straight in.
problem_bank.silver_description: Convert the units first (km, minutes or km/h), then substitute, or use the average speed.
